blocks.text: Trusted Legal Partners for Individuals, Families, and Businesses

At TNR Attorneys, we don’t just represent. We fight, advise, protect, and empower. Whether you have suffered a life-changing injury, faced an unlawful arrest, or need strategic legal support for your business, we are here to help you move forward with clarity and confidence.
We are based in South Africa and proudly serve clients across the country. Our clients range from individuals needing justice to companies seeking reliable legal partners.
“At TNR Attorneys, we measure success by the real impact we make in our clients’ lives.”— Toohey Rambau, Founding Partner
We believe in:
Access to justice for every client, regardless of status or background
Precision and preparation in every case we take on
Clear communication, with no jargon and no confusion

TNR Attorneys’ dedication to delivering favorable outcomes goes hand in hand with their commitment to upholding the dignity of each client they serve. This dual focus sets them apart as a reliable and compassionate legal team.
TNR Attorneys also stand out for their transparent fee structure, providing clients with clear and detailed information about the costs involved in their legal representation.
TNR Attorneys are renowned for their exceptional customer service, characterised by prompt responsiveness, clear communication, and a personalised approach to each client’s needs.
Frequently Asked Questions
Road Accident Fund (RAF) Claims

How long does an RAF claim take to settle? The timeline depends on the complexity of your injuries and the availability of medical reports. Some claims are finalised in two to three years, while others can take longer if they go to trial. At TNR, we focus on moving matters forward quickly and avoiding unnecessary delays.

What compensation can I receive from the RAF? Compensation may cover medical expenses, loss of income, long-term care needs, and general damages for pain and suffering. Each case is different, and we tailor the claim to your unique circumstances.
Do I have to pay legal fees upfront? No. In qualifying RAF cases, TNR Attorneys works on a “No Win, No Fee” basis. This means you only pay if we successfully secure compensation for you.
Medical Negligence

What counts as medical negligence? Medical negligence occurs when a healthcare professional fails to act with the reasonable standard of care, causing injury, harm, or complications that could have been avoided. Examples include misdiagnosis, surgical errors, or birth-related injuries.

How do you prove medical negligence? We work with independent medical experts who review your records, treatment, and outcomes. Their opinions help establish whether the care you received fell below acceptable standards.

Is it possible to sue a public hospital or clinic? Yes. Both public and private healthcare providers can be held accountable if negligence caused harm. Our role is to ensure that your rights are protected, no matter the institution.
Unlawful Arrest & Civil Rights

What is an unlawful arrest? An arrest is unlawful if it is carried out without proper legal grounds or without following due process. This often includes situations where police act outside their authority or misuse their powers.
What can I claim for if I was unlawfully arrested? You may claim compensation for loss of income, emotional trauma, reputational harm, and violation of your constitutional rights.
How long do I have to file a claim? Civil claims against the state are subject to strict timeframes. It is important to seek legal advice as soon as possible so that deadlines are not missed.
Commercial Disputes & Business Law

What is the benefit of having a lawyer review contracts? A lawyer ensures that your contracts protect your interests, reduce risks, and close loopholes that could lead to disputes later. Prevention is often far less costly than litigation.

How are shareholder disputes resolved? Shareholder disputes can be resolved through negotiation, mediation, or litigation. At TNR, we aim for solutions that protect both business stability and shareholder value.
Do you work with SMEs as well as large companies? Yes. We represent both small and medium enterprises and larger corporate clients. Each receives the same strategic, results-driven service.
Labour & Administrative Law
What is an unfair dismissal? An unfair dismissal occurs when an employee is terminated without fair reason or without following proper procedures, such as a disciplinary process.

Can employers also use your services? Yes. We guide employers on compliance with labour law, help draft contracts, and represent them in disciplinary hearings, CCMA proceedings, and bargaining council matters.

What is administrative law, and how does it affect me? Administrative law governs decisions made by public bodies, such as municipalities or government departments. If a decision unfairly affects you or your business, we can challenge it and ensure accountability.
Still have questions?
We are here to help. If you don’t see your question answered here, speak to one of our attorneys today.

title: COMMERCIAL LAW: PROTECTING COMMUNITY INTERESTS IN A LANDMARK LAND DEAL

title: Lessons from Dying Intestate: Why a Valid Will Matter

blocks.text: The Risk of Dying Without a Valid Will

In South Africa, dying intestate, that is, without leaving a valid will, results in the deceased’s estate being distributed in accordance with the Intestate Succession Act 81 of 1987. This statutory framework operates on a fixed formula, which often bears little resemblance to the wishes of the deceased. The surviving spouse is entitled to half of the estate and then on remaining half, the greater of R250,000 or a child’s share, while children share equally in the balance of the estate. Where minor children are left without a surviving parent, the Master of the High Court assumes responsibility for appointing a guardian. Cohabitating partners who are not legally married are excluded from succession altogether. Furthermore, the estate remains frozen until the Master formally appoints an executor, leaving dependents financially vulnerable during an already difficult time.
Consequences of Intestacy

The consequences of dying intestate extend beyond the rigid distribution of assets. Estate administration becomes immediately restricted, as no one may access or deal with the assets until an executor has been officially appointed by the Master. Families may find themselves in financial distress while awaiting this appointment, particularly where the deceased was the primary breadwinner. The result is a delay that compounds the hardship experienced by grieving dependents.
Avoiding the Pitfalls of Intestacy

The most effective means of avoiding these legal complications is the drafting of a valid will. By doing so, individuals ensure that their assets are distributed in accordance with their wishes rather than by statutory default. Legal advice is indispensable in this process, as an attorney can assist in ensuring that a will is drafted with clarity, validity, and enforceability. It is equally important to communicate these wishes with family members, thereby minimising the risk of conflict and disputes after death.
A Cautionary Tale: The Estate Battle of the Late Former Deputy President

The dangers of intestacy are aptly illustrated by the ongoing estate dispute involving the late former Deputy President. In adjudicating the matter, Judge Johannes Roelofse observed that such disputes frequently devastate families, leaving wounds that the deceased would likely never have intended. He implored the family to seek dialogue and reconciliation, while further emphasising that dependents of the deceased should not be left destitute or displaced. The case underscores the societal and familial consequences of inadequate estate planning and serves as a cautionary example of why careful preparation is indispensable.
The Protective Role of Pension Funds

Beyond wills and succession law, pension funds also provide critical safeguards to dependents. In terms of Section 7C(2) of the Pension Funds Act, fund boards are bound by fiduciary duties that require them to act with care, diligence, impartiality, and good faith. These duties extend to protecting the interests of members and beneficiaries, ensuring the financial soundness of funds, and avoiding conflicts of interest. In the context of intestacy, these statutory protections may serve as a vital safety net for dependents, ensuring continuity of support when estate disputes threaten financial stability.
How TNR Attorneys Inc. Can Assist

At TNR Attorneys Inc, we recognise the profound legal and personal implications of dying intestate. Our firm is dedicated to assisting clients with the drafting of valid wills that are legally sound, enforceable, and reflective of their true intentions. We also provide guidance on estate planning strategies, assist families with estate administration, and advise on pension fund benefit claims. In doing so, we seek to ensure that our clients’ wishes are honoured, and their families are spared the distress and uncertainty that inevitably accompany intestacy.

title: The Importance Of Understanding Marital Regimes Before Entering Into Marriage In South Africa

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Marriage is not only a union of hearts but also a legal and financial partnership governed by the laws of the Republic of South Africa. The choice of a marital regime determines how spouses’ assets, liabilities, and financial interests will be managed during the marriage and upon its dissolution through death or divorce. It is therefore imperative that couples understand the legal implications of each marriage regime before committing to marriage

South African matrimonial property law is primarily governed by the Matrimonial Property Act 88 of 1984, the Marriage Act 25 of 1961, and the Recognition of Customary Marriages Act 120 of 1998. These statutes provide the framework within which couples may determine their property relations.
2. Marriage In Community of Property

In a marriage in community of property, both spouses share a single, joint estate. Upon marriage, all assets and liabilities, whether acquired before or during the marriage, are combined. When the marriage is dissolved, either by divorce or death, the joint estate is divided equally between the spouses after all debts have been settled. While this system promotes equality, it also carries certain disadvantages. Both parties become jointly and severally liable for each other’s debts, and spousal consent is required for significant financial transactions such as:

items: The purchase or sale of immovable property;
The sale of shares or investment assets;
The signing of suretyship agreements; and
The withdrawal or transfer of funds from fixed deposits

blocks.text: This regime is the default marital system in South Africa unless the parties expressly agree otherwise by executing an antenuptial contract.
3. Marriage Out of Community of Property Without Accrual

A marriage out of community of property without accrual allows each spouse to retain full control over their individual assets and liabilities. This arrangement requires the parties to execute an Antenuptial Contract (ANC) before marriage. The ANC is a notarial deed that must be registered in the Deeds Office within three months of execution, or within six months if executed outside the Republic.

This regime follows the principle of ‘what is mine is mine, and what is yours is yours.’ Each spouse is responsible for their own debts and enjoys financial independence. It is particularly suitable for individuals who wish to protect personal or business assets from the financial risks of their partner.
However, recently the courts are empowered to exercise discretion on whether to accept the ANC or reject, each case depends on its own merits.
4. Marriage Out of Community of Property With Accrual
The accrual system is a hybrid approach that combines aspects of financial independence during the marriage with equitable sharing upon its dissolution. An ANC is also required for this regime.

Under this system, each spouse retains ownership of their individual estate during the marriage. However, upon dissolution, the spouse whose estate has shown the lesser growth (accrual) is entitled to share in the other’s estate to achieve a fair balance. The law excludes certain assets from the accrual calculation, such as:

items: Inheritances;
Donations;
Personal injury awards; and
Assets expressly excluded in the ANC.

blocks.text: This system promotes fairness by recognising the non-financial contributions of both spouses.
5. Customary and Cultural Considerations

Despite the legal clarity of marital regimes, there is ongoing debate regarding their interaction with African customary law and cultural practices. In traditional African marriages, lobola plays a significant role in validating the marriage.

Some cultural perspectives hold that executing an ANC before lobola negotiations contradicts customary norms, as lobola traditionally signifies the formal intention to marry. In Mbungela & Another v Mkabi & Others (2019) ZASCA 134, the Supreme Court of Appeal held that where there is clear evidence of intent to marry under customary law such as a letter of intent or partial payment of lobola the marriage may be deemed valid even if formalities were incomplete.
This demonstrates the courts’ flexible and context-sensitive approach to reconciling statutory and customary marriage principles.
6. Changing the Marital Regime

In terms of section 21 of the Matrimonial Property Act 88 of 1984, spouses may apply to the High Court to change their matrimonial property system after marriage. The application will only succeed if the following requirements are met:
1. Both parties consent to the change;
2. Creditors are notified and do not suffer prejudice; and
3. The new ANC is properly executed by a notary public and registered with the Deeds Office.
This ensures that the rights of third parties are protected while allowing couples to adjust their financial arrangements as circumstances evolve.
7. Conclusion

Regardless of cultural criticism or public debate such as discussions surrounding high-profile marriages like that of the artist Black Coffee the law remains clear and enforceable. If a couple intends to marry out of community of property, they must execute an Antenuptial Contract before the marriage takes place, irrespective of whether lobola has been fully or partially paid.

Failure to do so results in the marriage automatically defaulting to in community of property, with all its accompanying consequences. Understanding the different marital regimes is therefore essential for anyone entering into marriage in South Africa, as these choices have lifelong legal and financial implications.

title: Divorce in South Africa: It’s Not War… But It’s Not a Group Project Either

blocks.text: Introduction
We’ve all seen the movies. Someone throws a glass of expensive scotch, screams “I’ll see you in court!” and walks out into a waiting limousine.

In South Africa, the reality is usually a bit more… administrative. It involves less scotch-throwing and significantly more paperwork. If you’re at the point where “Netflix and Chill” has turned into “Separate Rooms and Silent Treatment,” it’s time to talk about the law.
Let’s be honest, nobody walks down the aisle thinking, “This will make a great court file one day.”
Yet divorce remains a reality for many South Africans. The key difference between a divorce that destroys lives and one that restores dignity often lies in one thing: information.
So let’s unpack divorce in South Africa, properly, factually, and without the courtroom drama you see on Moja Love.

items: The Law: What Actually Ends a Marriage?

blocks.text: In South Africa, divorce is governed primarily by the Divorce Act.
The Act recognises one main ground for divorce:
Irretrievable breakdown of the marriage.
That’s it.

items: Not “he forgot our anniversary.”
Not “she doesn’t like my mother.”
Not even “we argue about the remote.”

blocks.text: The court must be satisfied that the marriage relationship has broken down to such an extent that there is no reasonable prospect of restoration.
Examples include:

items: Separation for a continuous period
Adultery
Abuse
Complete breakdown of communication

blocks.text: You don’t need to prove someone is a villain. You need to show the marriage cannot be saved.
Divorce is not about punishment. It is about legal closure.

items: “But Who Gets What?” The Money Conversation Nobody Wants

blocks.text: Before people argue about the couches, they need to understand their marital regime.
Your marriage system is governed by the Matrimonial Property Act.
You are either:
🔹 Married In Community of Property
Everything (assets and debts) falls into one joint estate.
Yes, that includes the car. And the credit card.
🔹 Married Out of Community of Property (With Accrual)
Each spouse keeps their own estate, but growth during the marriage is shared at divorce.
🔹 Married Out of Community of Property (Without Accrual)
Each spouse walks away with what is legally theirs.
Here’s the uncomfortable truth:
Many people don’t know what regime they’re married under.
And that lack of knowledge becomes expensive.
3. Children Are Not “Assets” to Be Won
When children are involved, the court does not ask:
“Who is the better parent?”
The court asks:
“What is in the best interests of the child?”
This principle is entrenched in Section 28 of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa and further developed in the Children’s Act.
Important points:

items: Parental responsibilities and rights are not automatically removed because of divorce.
Contact is a right of the child, not a reward for the parent.
Maintenance is not optional, it is a legal obligation.
Children are not trophies. They are not leverage. They are human beings protected by law.

blocks.text: 4. Maintenance: It’s About Need, Not Revenge
Spousal maintenance is not automatic.
Under the Divorce Act, courts consider:

items: Financial needs
Earning capacity
Duration of the marriage
Standard of living during the marriage

blocks.text: Maintenance is not designed to “punish” the higher earner.
It exists to prevent unfair economic hardship.

items: That said, lifelong maintenance is rare unless circumstances justify it.

blocks.text: 5. Divorce Doesn’t Have to Be a Battlefield
There are generally two types of divorce:
🔹 Uncontested Divorce
Where parties agree on:

items: Asset division
Maintenance
Parenting plans

blocks.text: This is faster, cheaper, and far less emotionally damaging.
🔹 Contested Divorce
Where parties disagree.
This involves pleadings, possible trials, and higher costs.
Here’s something many people don’t realise:
Most divorces settle before trial.
Court should be the last resort and not the opening move.
6. The Emotional Reality No One Mentions
Divorce is not just a legal process. It is:

items: Financial restructuring
Emotional adjustment
Identity recalibration

blocks.text: Sometimes even social repositioning
People often say, “It’s just paperwork.”
It isn’t.
It’s paperwork that reorganises your entire life.
That’s why proper legal guidance matters , not just to win, but to transition.
7. Let’s Talk About the Conversation We Avoid
Here are questions worth asking:

items: Do you know what marital regime you’re married under?
Do you know what would happen to your pension if you divorced?
Do you know how maintenance is calculated?
Do you know your rights or are you operating on tik tok advice?

blocks.text: Divorce law is technical. Social media is loud. Only one of them is binding.
Final Thought: Divorce Is Not Failure but It Is a Legal Process
Marriage is a partnership.
Divorce is the legal dissolution of that partnership.
Handled correctly, it can:

items: Protect your dignity
Protect your children
Protect your financial future

blocks.text: Handled emotionally and without guidance, it can cause avoidable damage.
The law exists not to break families, but to regulate transitions fairly.
And sometimes, fairness is the most powerful form of closure
And remember in South Africa, the way you said “I do” determines how you say “Goodbye.”.
The Bottom Line
Divorce is rarely “fun,” but it doesn’t have to be a disaster. The goal isn’t to “win” a war; it’s to transition into your new life with your finances and your sanity intact.
Whether you’re looking for an amicable settlement or you need a robust team to protect your interests in a contested battle, TNR Attorneys is here to navigate the storm with you.

title: Wills vs. Trusts: Who’s Really Babysitting Your Legacy

blocks.text: Introduction

Planning for the “after-party” of life isn’t exactly a Sunday braai conversation. It’s a bit like buying insurance, you hope you never have to use it, but you’ll be glad you have it when “life” decides to happen. In South Africa, the difference between a Will and a Trust is the difference between leaving a map for your family and leaving them a GPS with a personal chauffeur and a full tank of petrol.

Let’s be honest, no one wakes up excited to plan what happens after they’re gone. It ranks somewhere between going to the dentist and trying to cancel a gym membership you swore you’d use. But if you have minor children, estate planning is not optional BUT it’s essential. And this is where the classic question comes in: Should you rely on a Will, or should you consider a Trust? A Will is often the starting point. Governed by the Wills Act 7 of 1953, it is the document that gives effect to your final wishes. It allows you to decide who inherits your assets, who will administer your estate, and who will take care of your children if they are still minors. In many ways, it gives you control on paper. However, the practical reality after death is governed by process. Your estate must be administered in terms of the Administration of Estates Act 66 of 1965, and where minor children are involved, things can become a little more complicated. A minor cannot legally inherit money outright. This means that, unless you have made alternative arrangements, their inheritance is typically paid into the Guardian’s Fund, administered by the Master of the High Court. While the Fund serves an important purpose and safeguards assets, accessing those funds can be a slow and administrative process. One might say it requires patience, paperwork, and a healthy respect for follow-ups. This is where a Trust quietly enters the conversation and, quite often, becomes the better long-term solution. A Trust, regulated by the Trust Property Control Act 57 of 1988, allows you to place assets under the control of trustees, who then manage those assets for the benefit of your chosen beneficiaries. When created in a Will (commonly referred to as a testamentary trust), it becomes a powerful tool for protecting minor children. Instead of assets being paid into a government administered fund, they are managed privately by individuals you have personally selected. These trustees can use the funds to provide for the child’s education, maintenance, and general wellbeing without the delays and formalities that often accompany institutional processes. Importantly, a Trust also allows you to decide when your child should receive full control of their inheritance. And while the law considers 18 to be the age of majority, many would agree that financial maturity does not always arrive on schedule. A Trust allows you to build in a measure of protection ensuring that the inheritance supports your child’s future, rather than funding a few enthusiastic but questionable life choices. It is worth noting that a Trust does not replace a Will. The two work together. YourWill sets everything in motion, it is the document that creates the Trust, appoints trustees, and directs how your estate should be handled. The Trust, in turn, ensures that your wishes are carried out in a controlled and practical manner long after your estate has been wound up. In practical terms, the difference can be significant. Without a Trust, a minor’s inheritance is subject to external administration and access constraints. With a Trust, the same assets are actively managed, readily available for the child’s needs, and protected in accordance with your instructions. Ultimately, estate planning is not about anticipating the worst but it is about preparing responsibly. It is about ensuring that, in your absence, your children are not left navigating unnecessary administrative hurdles, and that your assets continue to serve the purpose you intended. Because while many things in life can be left for “later,” this is not one of them. In fact, in both law and life, “I’ll deal with it later” has a way of becoming someone else’s problem, usually at the worst possible time. A Will is your entry ticket to being a responsible adult, but a Trust is your VIP pass to peace of mind. If you have children, property, or a business, relying on a Will alone is like wearing a belt with no trousers, technically you’re trying, but you’re still remarkably exposed. At TNR Attorneys, we regularly assist clients in structuring Wills and Trusts that are both legally sound and practically effective. Should you wish to explore what would best suit your circumstances, our team is available to guide you through the process with clarity and care.
